intro: This guide helps you lead twelve weekly sessions on Samuel Ajayi Crowther (For Children), the true story of a Yoruba boy who was sold as a slave, set free, came to know Jesus, gave his people the Bible in their own language, and became the first African bishop of the Anglican Church. It is written for children aged 6 to 12, and works just as well for a Sunday school class, a homeschool group or a family around the table.

Each session takes about thirty minutes. Welcome the children and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the week’s chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s short prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand so you know what is coming, and have paper and crayons or pencils ready. Some chapters tell of capture, separation and unfair treatment, so read those parts calmly and simply, let children ask what they need to, never press anyone to share their own hurts in front of the group, and keep coming back to the book’s steady message that God was with Ajayi all along.

weeks.summary: Ajayi is born about 1807 in Osogun, a busy walled Yoruba town in what is now Nigeria, where his father is a weaver and farmer and Ajayi leads a club of about forty boys who hoe the yam heaps together. His family prays to the old Yoruba gods and he knows nothing of Jesus, the sea or the wider world. The big idea: God saw Ajayi before he was born and had every day of his life in his book, and God sees each child too.

memory_verse.text: Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.

activity.title: A Page from God’s Book
steps: Give each child a sheet of paper folded in half like a book.
On the left page, have them draw Osogun: mud houses, tall roofs and a wooden fence with six gates.
On the right page, have them draw themselves at home or at play.
Help them write across the top, “God sees me,” and say the memory verse together while holding up the pictures.

weeks.summary: When Ajayi is about thirteen, in 1821, raiders attack Osogun; the family runs, his father is lost to him for ever, and Ajayi, his mother, sisters and a cousin are captured and led away. The chapter is honest that this was a terrible day, and that Ajayi later called it “the unhappy, but blessed day” because it began the road that led him to Jesus. The big idea: God does not call sad things good, but he stays with us and can bring good out of the hardest day; keep the telling calm and do not dwell on the details of the raid.

memory_verse.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.

activity.title: God Is Still With Me
steps: Stand in a circle and teach the reply: point up and say, “God is still with me!”
Call out times and places, such as “On my birthday,” “At school,” “When it’s dark,” “On a rainy day,” “When I feel sad.”
After each one, have everyone give the reply together, loud for happy times and soft for sad ones.
Finish by saying the memory verse together and reminding them that God was with Ajayi on his saddest day too.

weeks.summary: Ajayi is passed from owner to owner, traded once for a horse that was sent back, and sold about six times in all, each time further from home; he is taken past where his mother is kept without daring to call out, grows ill with sadness, and is finally carried across a great lagoon to Lagos, where the slave ships came. Read this gently and keep the focus on Ajayi’s feelings rather than on his hardships. The big idea: looking back, Ajayi saw that God had been watching over him and delivering him from evil the whole time, even before he knew God’s name.

memory_verse.text: The LORD will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul.

activity.title: “God Watches Over Me” Card
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
On the front, have them draw a big sun or a bright star shining over a small figure.
Inside, help them copy the words “God watches over me, even when I feel alone.”
Invite them to keep the card by their bed, and pray together for anyone who feels alone today.

weeks.summary: After nearly four months held in Lagos, Ajayi is put on a crowded Portuguese slave ship, but that very evening, 7 April 1822, two British warships stop it and the boys are taken onto the Myrmidon, where they mistake a hanging pig and cannonballs for something terrible and later laugh about it all their lives. The kind sailors feed and clothe them and bring them to Sierra Leone, where they are told, “You are free!” The big idea: Jesus came to set people free, and we can be like the sailors who helped people in trouble; the cannonball mix-up gives the children a welcome moment to laugh.

memory_verse.text: Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler’s snare. The snare is broken, and we have escaped.

activity.title: Map of Ajayi’s Journey
activity.materials: Large sheets of paper and crayons
steps: Put the children in groups of three or four with one large sheet of paper each.
Have them draw Osogun at the right side, a big blue lagoon with Lagos beside it, then the wide sea, and Sierra Leone on the far left.
Draw a dotted line from Osogun to Lagos, then add the British ship out at sea and a line to Sierra Leone.
Have them draw a flying bird over Sierra Leone and write “Free!” beside it, then say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: In the village of Bathurst in Sierra Leone, Ajayi lives with the missionary Mr. Davey and his wife, learns to read the New Testament in just six months, and is soon a paid monitor teaching younger children. He hears about Jesus, says “the Lord was pleased to open my heart,” and is baptised on 11 December 1825, taking the name Samuel Crowther while keeping his Yoruba name all his life; he later marries Asano, a girl rescued from another slave ship. The big idea: Jesus forgives us and makes us new on the inside, but we are still the person God made.

memory_verse.text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, they have become new.

activity.title: Little Monitors
steps: Explain that Ajayi was a monitor: as soon as he learned something, he taught it to someone else.
Teach the memory verse with simple hand actions, a line at a time, until the group knows it.
Put the children in pairs and have each one take a turn as the “monitor,” teaching the verse and actions to their partner.
Ask a few pairs to show the group, and cheer every monitor.

weeks.summary: Samuel becomes a teacher, the very first student at Fourah Bay College, and starts writing down Yoruba words. On the 1841 Niger River expedition a fever kills many Europeans while most Africans stay well, and Samuel writes that Africa will be helped most by “her own children”; in 1843 he is made a minister in London and comes home to lead a church service in Yoruba. The big idea: Jesus tells his friends to be his witnesses starting at home, so children can begin with the people right around them.

memory_verse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come on you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.

activity.title: Ripples from Home
activity.materials: One large sheet of paper and crayons
steps: Draw a small circle in the middle of the paper and write “Home” in it.
Draw bigger rings around it and label them “My street,” “My school,” “My town” and “The whole world.”
Ask the group for ways to share Jesus’ love in each ring, such as saying grace, inviting a friend to church, or praying for another country.
Write their ideas in the rings, then read the finished list aloud and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: In 1846 Samuel goes to live in Abeokuta among his own people, and within three weeks he learns that his mother is alive; on 21 August she comes, trembling, and after twenty-five years apart they hold each other in tearful silence while she calls him by his childhood pet names. She has had a hard life as a slave, but she learns about Jesus, is baptised Hannah in 1848, and gladly lets her son go to serve God. The big idea: God did not forget Samuel or his mother, and he does not forget us; be aware that some children may be apart from a parent and keep the talk warm and general.

memory_verse.text: Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!

activity.title: A Thank-You Card for Someone Who Cares
steps: Have each child fold a sheet of paper to make a card.
Ask them to think quietly of someone who looks after them: a parent, grandparent, carer, teacher or friend.
On the front, have them draw a picture for that person; inside, help them write “Thank you for caring for me” and sign their name.
Finish by thanking God together that he never forgets any of us, and let them take the card home to give.

weeks.summary: Hardly anyone had written Yoruba down, so Samuel works out how to spell it, writes a book to teach it, and leads the team that translates the Bible, finished in 1884 after more than forty years. On a visit to England in 1851 he meets Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle, where she lights the candles herself when the lamp goes out, and he prays the Lord’s Prayer in Yoruba, which she says sounds “soft and melodious.” The big idea: God loves every language and wants every people to hear about Jesus in the words they understand best.

memory_verse.text: How do we hear, everyone in our own native language?

activity.title: The Night the Lamp Went Out
activity.materials: Nothing (a sheet of paper can be the map)
steps: Choose children to play Samuel, Prince Albert and Queen Victoria, with everyone else as guests in the room.
Act out the scene: Samuel and the Prince look at a map, the Queen comes in quietly, the lamp goes out, and the Queen pretends to light the candles.
When a guest asks Samuel to say something in his own language, have the whole group stand and pray the Lord’s Prayer together.
Invite any child who knows another language to say “Amen” or “thank you” in it, if they would like to.

weeks.summary: Samuel travels the Niger again and again; in 1854 the Pleiad returns after more than a hundred days with no one dead, and in 1857 he leaves two African helpers to start a church at Onitsha before the Dayspring hits rocks near Jebba and tips over, with everyone getting safely ashore. Fifty people camp by the river for a whole year, and Samuel leads prayers morning and evening, cares for the sick, laughs at himself when a leopard visits (“I am no gunner”), and learns and writes down the Nupe language. The big idea: when things go wrong, keep trusting God and keep doing good, because God can use even our worst days.

memory_verse.text: Let us not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.

activity.title: Don’t Give Up Walk
activity.materials: One sheet of paper per child
steps: Line the children up along one wall with a sheet of paper balanced flat on each head.
Have them walk slowly to the other side of the room without touching the paper.
If a paper falls, have the child pick it up, put it back, say “Don’t give up!” and keep going from that spot.
When everyone has crossed, cheer together and say the memory verse.

weeks.summary: The missionaries in London decide the Niger churches need an African bishop and choose Samuel, who says “I am not worthy” but at last agrees: “It is the Lord; let Him do what seemeth Him good.” On 29 June 1864 at Canterbury Cathedral he becomes the first African bishop of the Anglican Church, and his old teacher Mrs. Davey, now Mrs. Weeks, refuses to give up her seat because she taught him his alphabet; yet the new bishop asks not to be called “My Lord” and gives his own chair to a schoolteacher. The big idea: God loves to lift up the humble, and we only need to say yes to him.

memory_verse.text: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

activity.title: The Bishop’s Chair
steps: Put one chair in the middle of the room and choose a child to be Bishop Samuel sitting in it.
Have another child knock and come in as the schoolteacher, and let the bishop stand and offer the chair with a smile.
Swap so several children get a turn at offering the seat.
Ask the group to name other ways to put someone else first this week, like letting someone go first or sharing the best spot.

weeks.summary: In 1867 Bishop Crowther and his son Dandeson are seized by Chief Abokko, who wrongly thinks the bishop is rich and demands a huge payment; the chief’s own slaves secretly share their food, a cloth and a robe, and Samuel says they are like the ravens God sent to feed Elijah. On Sunday he bravely asks for his Bible back and gets it, Dandeson refuses to leave his father, and they finally escape to a steamer, though their helper Mr. Fell is killed by an arrow; mention his death briefly and gently. The big idea: God cared for Samuel through the small kindness of poor people, and a small kindness can be God’s answer to someone’s prayer.

memory_verse.text: The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.

activity.title: A Flock of Kindness Ravens
steps: Have each child draw a big black bird, a raven, on a sheet of paper.
Inside or beside the bird, help them write or draw one small kindness they will do this week, like sharing, helping or including someone.
Lay all the ravens together on the floor or a wall to make a flock.
Pray together that God would use each small kindness to answer someone’s prayer.

weeks.summary: Samuel’s children love his stories, especially the one about his first heavy boots, when he had to hold the wall to walk round the room. In old age his wife Asano dies and young missionaries unfairly push aside African ministers, even his own son, which the Church of England much later admitted was wrong, but Samuel does not fight back and keeps loving and serving. On the last night of 1891 he tells his daughter Abigail “Good night” and goes peacefully home to Jesus. The big idea: Samuel trusted God on happy and sad days alike and could rest in peace because he knew he was safe with God; this is a good week to look back over the whole story.

memory_verse.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, the LORD alone, make me live in safety.

activity.title: Story Line-Up
activity.materials: Eight sheets of paper and a crayon, prepared by the leader
steps: Before the session, write one moment on each sheet: “Born in Osogun,” “The ship is stopped,” “A new name,” “Mother!”, “The Bible in Yoruba,” “The shipwreck year,” “Made a bishop,” “Good night.”
Mix up the sheets and give them to eight children to hold.
Have the rest of the group help them stand in the right order, telling a little of each part of the story as they go.
Finish by walking down the line together and saying “God was with him” at each sheet.
